title: Merge, Rebase, and Cherry-Pick
intro: Three ways to move commits between branches, with very different effects on history — and on what your pipeline builds.

steps.prompt: Update your feature branch with the latest main by merging it in.
steps.fake_output:
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 src/api.js | 12 ++++++------
 1 file changed
steps.explanation: A merge commit ties the two histories together; nothing existing is rewritten.
steps.why: Merging is always safe on shared branches because it never changes existing commits. The cost is a busier history with merge commits.

steps.prompt: Alternatively, replay your feature commits on top of the latest main to keep history linear.
steps.explanation: Your commits are recreated on top of main with NEW hashes — history looks as if you'd started from the latest main.
steps.why: The golden rule: only rebase commits nobody else has pulled. Rebasing a shared branch rewrites history others have built on, and their next pull turns into a mess. After rebasing a branch you already pushed, you need 'git push --force-with-lease' (never plain --force).

steps.prompt: Before opening a PR, squash your last 3 messy work-in-progress commits into one clean commit.
steps.fake_output:
(editor opens)
pick c3d4e5f fix cart total rounding
squash d4e5f6a wip
squash e4f5a6b wip again

Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/cart.
steps.explanation: Interactive rebase lets you squash, reorder, reword, or drop commits.
steps.why: One clean commit per logical change makes 'git revert' and 'git bisect' far more useful later — reverting a single well-scoped commit is easy; untangling 'wip' commits during an incident isn't.

steps.prompt: A security fix (commit 7a8b9c0) was merged to main, but also needs to go onto the release/2.3 branch without bringing any other main changes along.
steps.fake_output:
[release/2.3 f1e2d3c] fix: sanitize coupon input
 1 file changed, 4 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
steps.explanation: The same change is applied as a new commit on the release branch.
steps.why: Cherry-pick is the standard way to backport hotfixes to maintained release branches. Use 'git cherry-pick -x' to record the original commit hash in the message, so it's traceable later.
